title: Where a System Gets Cut
voice: Pablo Macias (es-MX), calmo y claro, ritmo de clase

lines.text: Sysops Squad, the technical support arm of the electronics company, stores its customers' credit cards in its ticketing system, to charge them for their monthly plan.
Because of that, it may have to pass a PCI audit, which is the security standard for anyone who stores card data.
And the bigger the part of the system that touches those cards, the heavier the audit gets.
So the team proposes separating billing from the rest. It would become an isolated zone that the other parts of the system cannot call directly.
A security reason, and the cost of an audit, decides where a boundary goes.
Where a system gets cut into parts is one of the decisions that costs the most to change later. And there is an order that keeps repeating.
The business proposes the parts, what each part needs decides where each cut goes, and only after that is the style chosen.
One technique for finding the parts is event storming. You write down everything that happens in the business, in the past tense and in order.
In MonitorMe, for example: a sensor reading arrived, a problem was detected, an alert was sent, the nurse saw the alert.
Then those facts are grouped by business process, and each group is a zone where every word has a single meaning.
The same exercise helps decide what stays out. MonitorMe left the sensors themselves out, with a written decision.
And it kept the patient registry inside, but as a supporting part that gets no focus, also in writing.
Taking something out of scope, or deciding it gets no effort, is also a cut.
The business supplies the candidates, but the written reason for each cut is usually something else: what that part needs. Sysops Squad shows it with its four areas.
The customer area, where tickets are opened and the profile is edited, needs to be available and respond quickly.
The operations area needs the technician, already at the customer's home, to find the ticket and the knowledge base.
The billing area needs security, because a leak of cards, they write, could have legal consequences.
And the administration area, with reports and user management, tolerates delays, because nothing serious happens if a report takes a bit longer. Each boundary ends up where the need changes.

scenes.kicker: Also deciding what not to split

lines.text: There is another way to decide each cut, and it comes from Farmacy Family, a health community that improves the Farmacy Food system.
Its team used a table. For each feature they noted, among other things, how much the code changes, how much it has to scale, and how sensitive its data is.
With that table they separated, in almost all the domains, the administration part from the customer part.
And in one they decided the opposite. Authentication and authorization stayed together, in the same piece, because the system needs both and cannot operate if one goes down.
Separating them would only add cost. In other words, not splitting is also a decision, and it is written with the same reasoning as a cut.

scenes.kicker: What calls each other stays together

lines.text: There is one more criterion, and it has to do with how the parts call each other.
If a service has to wait for another's response before it can continue, the two depend on each other, and if one goes down, the other cannot respond either.

Spotlight, the job platform that asked for between three and four nines, grouped the services that call each other this way into a single unit, which it calls a quantum. And that let it ask each unit for what it needs.
The ones that don't depend on others in that way, like reports, aim for three nines of availability. The ones that do, like notifications, aim for four.
With a single number for the whole system, and this is our own reading, four nines would have to be paid for everywhere.

With the parts defined, what remains is choosing how they are deployed and how they communicate, which is the style. Farmacy Food chose a modular monolith, which is a single application divided internally into modules with clear boundaries.
Its reason has to do with the state of the business. Microservices preferably call for a stable, well-known domain model, and the team writes that for its ordering system this does not apply.
Microservices, they say, should grow as they become necessary. The cost is also written down: it takes discipline so the modules don't get mixed together.
And the condition for splitting a module was noted: that the metrics show it is under more pressure than the others.
Sysops Squad's billing, isolated, shrinks the part of the system that touches cards. But the cut immediately brings a question.
If the card is no longer in the customer's part, how does the customer see it to edit it? The team answers in writing: seeing the last four digits is enough.
A cut decided by security exposed another decision, which part of the system stores each piece of data and what the others see.
